passages.title: The Pencil Case
text: The pencil case went missing on a Wednesday, and by Thursday everybody knew that Devan had taken it.

Nobody had seen him take it. That was not the point. The point was that the pencil case was new and expensive and belonged to Sara, and that Devan's own pencil case was a plastic bag with three stubs of pencil in it, and that he sat two seats away.
By Friday, four people had stopped lending him things.
I did not join in, but I did not say anything either, which I have since learnt is a decision and not the absence of one.

On Monday, Mrs Rajan asked the class to stay behind for five minutes. She did not mention the pencil case. She said that she had lost her reading glasses on Friday and had spent the weekend certain that she had left them at the hawker centre, and that she had been quite rude to the stallholder about it on the telephone.
Then she took the glasses out of her own desk drawer, where they had been the whole time.
"I have written her a letter," she said. "It is not a good letter. There is no good letter for that."
She let us think about it for a moment, and then she said we could go.
The pencil case turned up on Tuesday, behind the cupboard, where it had fallen through the gap at the back of Sara's shelf.

Nobody apologised to Devan. Not one of us, including me. He came back to school on Wednesday and everything carried on as though the week had not happened, and within a fortnight I think most people had genuinely forgotten.

I have not forgotten. I am thirty-one, and I still think about the plastic bag with the three pencil stubs in it, and about how quickly we decided, and about how easy it would have been to say one sentence on the Friday.
I have said the sentence a few times since, in other rooms, about other people. It is never easy. But it is always easier than remembering that you did not.

questions.q: Why did the class decide that Devan had taken the pencil case? (2m)
questions.a: Because the pencil case was new and valuable while Devan's own was only a plastic bag containing three pencil stubs, and because he sat close to Sara — so they assumed he had both a motive and the opportunity.
questions.tip: Two marks: the poverty assumption and the seating. Note that nobody actually saw anything.

questions.q: What does the narrator mean by "I did not say anything either, which I have since learnt is a decision and not the absence of one"? (2m)
questions.a: He means that staying silent was itself a choice with consequences, not a neutral act, and that by saying nothing he allowed the accusation to continue.
questions.tip: The whole passage turns on this sentence. Explain it fully.

questions.q: Why did Mrs Rajan tell the class the story about her reading glasses? (3m)
questions.a: Firstly, she wanted to show that she too had accused somebody without evidence. In addition, by using herself as the example she avoided naming Devan or embarrassing the class directly. Finally, her story demonstrated that such an accusation causes real harm that an apology cannot fully undo.
questions.tip: Three marks. The third point comes from her remark about the letter.

questions.q: What did Mrs Rajan mean by "There is no good letter for that"? (2m)
questions.a: She meant that no apology, however carefully written, can undo the hurt of having been wrongly accused, so the letter would always be inadequate.

questions.q: Where was the pencil case found, and why is this detail important? (2m)
questions.a: It had fallen through a gap at the back of Sara's shelf and was behind the cupboard. It matters because it proves nobody had taken it at all, so the entire accusation had been built on assumption.
questions.tip: Answer both halves — the location and its significance.

questions.q: "Nobody apologised to Devan." Why do you think this was? (2m)
questions.a: Because admitting they had been wrong would have meant facing their own unfairness, and it was easier for the class to let the matter quietly drop than to confront what they had done.
questions.tip: 'Why do you think' — inference, not a stated reason.

questions.q: How do we know the incident affected the narrator more than the others? (3m)
questions.a: Firstly, he says that within a fortnight most people had forgotten, but that he has not. In addition, he is now thirty-one and still recalls the exact detail of the plastic bag and the three pencil stubs. Finally, he says he has since spoken up in other situations, showing the incident permanently changed how he behaves.
questions.tip: Three marks, three pieces of evidence across the last two paragraphs.

questions.q: Explain the final sentence: "It is never easy. But it is always easier than remembering that you did not." (2m)
questions.a: He means that speaking up against unfairness is always uncomfortable, but that the discomfort lasts only a moment, whereas the guilt of having stayed silent stays with you for years.
questions.tip: Link it back to the fact that he is still thinking about this at thirty-one.

passages.title: Why Cities Are Getting Hotter
text: On a still afternoon, the centre of a large city can be as much as seven degrees warmer than the countryside a few kilometres away. Scientists call this the urban heat island effect, and Singapore experiences one of the strongest examples in the world.

The causes are mostly matters of material. Concrete, asphalt and brick absorb heat during the day and release it slowly through the night, which is why city nights cool down far less than rural ones. A dark road surface can reach sixty degrees in the afternoon sun. Grass in the same conditions stays close to air temperature, because plants release water vapour through their leaves, and evaporation cools the air around them.

Shape matters as well as material. Tall buildings standing close together trap heat between them in what researchers call an urban canyon. Heat that would otherwise radiate upwards into the sky bounces instead from wall to wall. The same buildings block the wind that would carry warm air away.

Then there is the heat we generate ourselves. Every air conditioner cools a room by moving heat outdoors. Every vehicle engine, every kitchen, every server room adds warmth to the street. On the hottest days, when air conditioners are working hardest, this contribution is at its greatest — which means the problem worsens precisely when it is least welcome.

The consequences are not merely uncomfortable. Higher night temperatures disturb sleep, and poor sleep affects health and concentration. Elderly residents and those without air conditioning are most at risk. Energy use rises, which in turn generates more heat.

There are remedies, though none is a complete answer. Planting trees along streets provides shade and evaporative cooling at the same time. Roofs painted white or planted with vegetation absorb far less heat than dark ones. Designing new estates so that buildings channel rather than block the prevailing wind can lower street temperatures measurably.
None of these measures will make a tropical city cool. What they can do is prevent it from becoming several degrees hotter than it needs to be, which over a lifetime is not a small difference.

questions.q: How much warmer can a city centre be than nearby countryside? (1m)
questions.a: As much as seven degrees warmer.
questions.tip: Literal. One line.

questions.q: Explain, in your own words, why grass stays cooler than a road surface. (2m)
questions.a: Plants give off water vapour from their leaves, and as that moisture evaporates it draws heat out of the surrounding air, keeping the temperature near the grass close to that of the air itself.
questions.tip: 'Evaporation cools' must be reworded, not lifted.

questions.q: What is an 'urban canyon' and why does it make a city hotter? (2m)
questions.a: It is the narrow space formed between tall buildings that stand close together. Heat that would normally escape upwards is reflected from one wall to another instead, and the buildings also block the wind that would otherwise remove the warm air.
questions.tip: Two marks: define it, then give the effect.

questions.q: What does the word 'radiate' mean in paragraph 3?
questions.a: Spread outwards or be given off.
questions.tip: A synonym that fits the sentence grammatically.

questions.q: Why does the writer say the problem "worsens precisely when it is least welcome"? (2m)
questions.a: Because air conditioners push heat out into the street, and they are used most heavily on the hottest days, so the outdoor temperature is pushed up further at exactly the time when people are already suffering most from the heat.
questions.tip: Explain the irony the phrase is pointing at.

questions.q: Give two consequences of higher night temperatures. (2m)
questions.a: People sleep badly, which damages their health and their ability to concentrate. Energy use also increases as more cooling is needed, and that in turn produces still more heat.
questions.tip: Two distinct consequences from paragraph 5.

questions.q: Explain how planting street trees helps in two different ways. (2m)
questions.a: Firstly, the trees cast shade so that surfaces beneath them absorb less heat from the sun. Secondly, they release water vapour from their leaves, and the evaporation cools the surrounding air.
questions.tip: The passage says 'at the same time' — that signals two mechanisms.

questions.q: What is the writer's attitude in the final paragraph? Explain using the text. (3m)
questions.a: Firstly, the writer is realistic rather than optimistic, admitting openly that no measure is a complete answer and that a tropical city cannot be made cool. In addition, he still argues the remedies are worth pursuing, since they can stop the city becoming several degrees hotter than necessary. Finally, the phrase 'over a lifetime is not a small difference' shows he considers the gain genuinely important despite being modest.
questions.tip: Three marks: name the attitude, support it twice.

passages.title: The Understudy
text: I was cast as the understudy, which in our school production meant learning every line of a part I would almost certainly never perform.

The lead was Priyanka. She had been the lead in everything since Primary Three, and she was, to be fair about it, extremely good. She did not gloat. She once spent a whole lunchtime helping me with a line I kept dropping, which made it harder rather than easier to resent her.

I learnt the part anyway. Forty-one pages. I learnt it in the shower, on the bus, in the eleven minutes between finishing dinner and starting homework. My mother could recite two of the scenes by the third week.
On the afternoon of the second performance, Priyanka's grandfather died.
Mrs Sundaram found me in the corridor at four o'clock and told me, and then asked whether I was ready, and I said yes before I had decided whether it was true.

I would like to report that it went brilliantly. It went adequately. I dropped a line in the second act and covered it clumsily, and my voice did something strange during the speech I had practised most. Nobody in the audience knew any different, because nobody in the audience had seen Priyanka do it the night before.
But I knew.

Afterwards, a parent I did not know told me I had been wonderful, and I said thank you, and I meant the thank you and did not believe the compliment, and I have since discovered that this is a fairly ordinary adult experience.

Priyanka came back the following week. She had watched a recording. She said three specific things about my performance, two of them generous and one of them accurate, and the accurate one was about the speech where my voice had gone strange.
"You were pushing," she said. "You don't have to push. It's already loud enough in there."
I have thought about that more than I have thought about the performance.

I did not become an actor. I stand up in front of rooms for a living, though, which is a related skill, and every time I feel myself pushing I hear a twelve-year-old telling me that the room is already quiet and I do not need to fill it.

questions.q: What did being the understudy involve? (1m)
questions.a: Learning every line of the lead part despite being almost certain never to perform it.

questions.q: Why does the narrator say Priyanka's kindness "made it harder rather than easier"? (2m)
questions.a: Because if she had been arrogant he could have resented her, but her generosity in helping him removed that excuse and left him with nothing but his own disappointment.
questions.tip: The difficulty is emotional, not practical.

questions.q: Give two details that show how hard the narrator worked. (2m)
questions.a: He learnt all forty-one pages, using every spare moment such as time in the shower, on the bus and between dinner and homework. His mother heard it so often that she could recite two scenes herself by the third week.
questions.tip: Two separate pieces of evidence.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention that nobody in the audience had seen Priyanka perform the night before? (2m)
questions.a: To explain that the audience had nothing to compare his performance with, so they could not tell it was weaker — which is why only he knew how it had really gone.
questions.tip: It sets up the two-word paragraph that follows.

questions.q: What is the effect of the two-word paragraph "But I knew."? (2m)
questions.a: Its shortness makes it land heavily after the longer paragraph before it, and it shifts the focus from the audience's judgement to his own, which is the one that actually matters to him.
questions.tip: Comment on both the form and the meaning.

questions.q: Explain what the narrator means by "I meant the thank you and did not believe the compliment". (2m)
questions.a: He was sincerely grateful that the parent had bothered to be kind, but he did not accept that the praise was deserved, because he knew the performance had only been adequate.
questions.tip: Two halves to the sentence — deal with both.

questions.q: Priyanka said three things, "two of them generous and one of them accurate". What does this tell us about her? (3m)
questions.a: Firstly, it shows she was kind enough to offer encouragement before criticism. In addition, it shows she was honest enough to say the one thing that was true rather than only what was comfortable. Finally, the fact that the accurate comment was about the exact moment he knew had gone wrong shows she was a genuinely perceptive judge of performance.
questions.tip: Three marks. The third point comes from matching her comment to his own private knowledge.

questions.q: Explain the final paragraph and why it is an effective ending. (4m)
questions.a: Firstly, it moves the story decades forward and reveals that the narrator now speaks publicly for a living. In addition, it shows Priyanka's advice about not pushing turned out to apply far beyond acting. Furthermore, describing her as 'a twelve-year-old' emphasises how young she was to have understood something he still uses as an adult. Finally, the ending gives the lasting value of the experience not to the performance itself but to one sentence of honest feedback, which quietly reverses what the reader expected the story to be about.
questions.tip: Four marks. Save the strongest point — the reversal — for last.

passages.title: The Second Language
text: My grandmother and I have never had a conversation.

This is not a figure of speech. She speaks Teochew and a little Mandarin. I speak English and the kind of Mandarin that collapses the moment anybody says something I have not heard before. Between us we have perhaps two hundred words, and about forty of them are food.

For most of my childhood this did not strike me as a loss. She was the person who appeared on Sundays with a tin of kueh and sat in the corner of the living room while the adults talked. She smiled at me. I smiled at her. Somebody translated when it mattered.
Two years ago my mother mentioned, in passing, that my grandmother had been a schoolteacher in Chaozhou before she came here, and that she had taught for eleven years.
I did not know this. I was twenty-four.

I have since found out, in fragments, through my mother, that she taught mathematics, that she walked forty minutes each way to the school, and that she stopped teaching when she moved here because her qualifications were not recognised and her English was not good enough. She worked in a factory that made electrical switches for nineteen years.
None of this is a secret. Nobody hid it. It simply never came up, because the person it belonged to could not tell me herself, and I had never thought to ask anybody else.
I have started learning Teochew. I am extremely bad at it. I have a notebook and an app and a cousin in Penang who sends me voice messages I understand perhaps a third of.

Last month I managed a full sentence. I asked her whether the kueh was difficult to make. She looked at me for a long moment — long enough that I thought I had said something else entirely — and then she laughed, and answered, and I understood almost none of the answer.
But she answered for a long time. Longer than the question deserved. She was still going when my mother came in from the kitchen.
I am thirty-one years behind. She is eighty-four. I am aware of the arithmetic.
I am learning it anyway.

questions.q: Why have the narrator and her grandmother never had a conversation? (2m)
questions.a: Because they share almost no common language — the grandmother speaks Teochew and a little Mandarin, while the narrator speaks English and only very limited Mandarin, leaving them with around two hundred shared words.
questions.tip: The reason is stated but should be reworded.

questions.q: What is the effect of the detail that "about forty of them are food"? (2m)
questions.a: It is quietly humorous, but it also shows how narrow their shared vocabulary is — limited almost entirely to practical, everyday matters rather than anything personal.
questions.tip: Comment on tone as well as meaning.

questions.q: Why did the narrator not see the situation as a loss when she was a child? (2m)
questions.a: Because as a child she accepted the arrangement as normal: her grandmother was simply a familiar presence who brought food and smiled, and an adult translated whenever something important needed saying.
questions.tip: 'Why' — start with 'Because'.

questions.q: Summarise what the narrator later learnt about her grandmother's life. (3m)
questions.a: Firstly, she had been a mathematics teacher in Chaozhou for eleven years, walking forty minutes each way to work. In addition, she gave up teaching on moving to Singapore because her qualifications were not accepted here and her English was insufficient. Finally, she then spent nineteen years working in a factory making electrical switches.
questions.tip: Three marks means three distinct facts.

questions.q: "None of this is a secret. Nobody hid it." Explain why the narrator did not know it. (2m)
questions.a: Because the one person whose life it was could not tell her directly, owing to the language barrier, and it had never occurred to the narrator to ask anyone else about it.
questions.tip: Both halves matter — the barrier and her own failure to ask.

questions.q: Why do you think the grandmother "looked at her for a long moment" before laughing? (2m)
questions.a: Because she was surprised to be addressed in her own language by her granddaughter for the first time, and she needed a moment to take in both the sentence and what it meant that it had been attempted.
questions.tip: 'Why do you think' — inference.

questions.q: Why does the writer say the grandmother answered "longer than the question deserved"? (3m)
questions.a: Firstly, the question was a very simple one about making kueh, so a short reply would have been enough. In addition, the length of the answer suggests the grandmother was delighted to be spoken to and wanted the exchange to continue. Finally, it hints at how much she may have wanted to say over the years and never been able to.
questions.tip: Three marks. Build from the literal to the emotional.

questions.q: Explain the last three short paragraphs and what they show about the narrator. (3m)
questions.a: Firstly, she states plainly that she is thirty-one years behind and that her grandmother is eighty-four, acknowledging she may have very little time. In addition, 'I am aware of the arithmetic' shows she has faced the likelihood that she will never become fluent enough for a real conversation. Finally, 'I am learning it anyway' shows she has decided the attempt is worth making regardless of whether it succeeds, which is the point of the whole passage.
questions.tip: Three very short paragraphs — the brevity is deliberate. Explain the progression.

listening3.title: Listening Comprehension · Practice Paper 3
listening3.instructions: An adult reads each text aloud TWICE at a normal pace, with a short pause between the two readings. The child reads the question and the four options first. Do not show the child the script. 20 marks.

items.script: Attention all pupils. The Primary Five swimming carnival scheduled for this Thursday has been brought forward to Wednesday because of the weather forecast. Pupils should bring their swimming attire on Wednesday instead. Thursday will follow the normal timetable.
items.q: What has happened to the swimming carnival?
options: It has been moved one day earlier
It has been moved one day later
It will run on both days

items.script: Girl: Did you manage to book the badminton court? Boy: Only the eight o'clock slot was left. Girl: Eight in the morning? On a Saturday? Boy: I know. But it was that or nothing until next month.
items.q: Why did the boy book that particular slot?
options: It was the only one available
It was the earliest he could wake up

items.script: Please note that the pedestrian crossing outside the main gate will be repainted on Friday morning. Pupils arriving before nine should use the overhead bridge instead. Teachers will be stationed at both ends of the bridge to direct traffic.
items.q: What should pupils do on Friday morning?

items.script: Boy: My father says I can adopt the kitten, but only if I pay for the vaccinations myself. Girl: How much is that? Boy: About ninety dollars. I have sixty-two saved, so I need another month of pocket money.
items.q: How much more does the boy need?

items.script: The following books are due for return this week: all titles borrowed before the June holidays. Titles borrowed during the holidays are due at the end of the month. Pupils with overdue items will not be able to borrow again until the items are returned.
items.q: When are holiday borrowings due?
options: At the end of the month

items.script: Woman: Is this the queue for the tickets? Man: For the matinee, yes. If you want the evening show the counter is upstairs. Woman: Oh. Is the matinee sold out? Man: Not yet, but there are only a few seats near the front left.
items.q: What does the man tell the woman about the matinee?
options: Only a few front-left seats remain

items.script: Today's cooking tip. When boiling eggs, start them in cold water rather than dropping them into water that is already boiling. Bring the pan slowly to the boil, then turn off the heat and leave them covered. This prevents the shells from cracking and gives a more even result.
items.q: Why should eggs start in cold water?
options: It stops the shells cracking and cooks them evenly
It makes them easier to peel

items.script: Girl: I've been picked for the debate team. Boy: That's brilliant. Girl: I'm not sure. I said yes before I thought about it, and now I have to speak in front of two hundred people in three weeks. Boy: You'll be fine. Girl: That is exactly what my mother said, and it did not help either.
items.q: How does the girl feel?

items.script: Visitors are reminded that the orchid conservatory is kept at a lower temperature than the rest of the gardens. A light jacket is recommended. Photography is permitted but tripods are not, as the walkways are narrow and become congested at weekends.
items.q: Why are tripods not allowed?
options: The walkways are narrow and get crowded

items.script: Boy: Why is the recycling bin full of ordinary rubbish again? Girl: Somebody put a whole bag of food waste in it yesterday. Girl: Now the entire bin has to go to the incinerator. Boy: So all the paper people sorted was wasted. Girl: That's exactly the problem.
items.q: What is the consequence of the contaminated bin?
options: Everything in it must be incinerated

items.script:
Good afternoon. I'm here to explain how the Primary Six buddy reading programme will work this year, because it is a little different from last year.

Each of you will be paired with a Primary One pupil. You will meet twice a week, on Tuesday and Thursday, during the second half of recess. That gives you about fifteen minutes each session. Fifteen minutes does not sound long, and it isn't, which is why preparation matters.

Here is the change. Last year you chose the books. This year your buddy chooses, from a shelf of about sixty titles in the library corner. Some of you will find this frustrating. You may end up reading the same book about a truck eleven times. That is normal, and it is not a failure. Young children reread because rereading is how they build confidence.

Your job is not to correct every mistake. If your buddy says a word wrongly but the sentence still makes sense, let it go. If the sentence stops making sense, wait three seconds, then help. Three seconds feels like a very long time. Count it in your head.

Finally, keep the record card. One line per session: the title, and one thing your buddy did well. Not what they got wrong. One thing they did well. Hand it in at the end of term.
items.q: How often will the buddies meet?
What is different from last year?
options: The Primary One pupil chooses the book

items.q: Why does the speaker say rereading the same book is normal?
options: Because rereading helps young children build confidence

items.q: When should a reader step in to help?
options: After three seconds, if the sentence no longer makes sense
Only at the end of the page

items.q: What must be written on the record card?
options: The title and one thing the buddy did well

items.script:
Interviewer: You've repaired shoes on this street for forty-one years. Is the trade dying?

Mr Teo: Everybody asks me that. The honest answer is that it changed, and then it changed back a little.

Interviewer: Changed back?

Mr Teo: In the nineties, nobody repaired anything. A shoe broke, you bought another shoe. My busiest years were the sixties and seventies, and then it went very quiet for about twenty years. I nearly closed twice.

Interviewer: And now?

Mr Teo: Now I have young customers. Twenty-five, thirty years old. They bring me expensive boots and they want them to last. Some of them ask me to teach them. I have taught four people, and three of them gave up within a month, which is about the usual rate.

Interviewer: Why do they give up?

Mr Teo: Because they expect to be good at it. Nobody is good at it. I was not good at it for six years. My teacher let me resole practice shoes that were going to be thrown away anyway, and he never once told me I was doing well, because I was not.

Interviewer: That sounds harsh.

Mr Teo: It was accurate. There is a difference. When I finally did something properly he said one word, and I have remembered that word for forty years. If he had said it every week it would have been worth nothing.
items.q: How long has Mr Teo repaired shoes?
When was the trade at its quietest?
options: Roughly the nineties onwards for twenty years

items.q: Who are his new customers?
options: Younger adults who want expensive shoes to last

items.q: Why does he say most learners give up?
options: They expect to be good at it quickly
There is no space in the shop

items.q: What point is he making about his own teacher's praise?
options: Rare, honest praise meant far more than frequent praise would have
Praise does not matter at all
